utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today's Thursday, the 8th of May, 2008. My greetings to the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and to all the people helping us out. We have to continue with the examination-in-chief of the witness. Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, there is a housekeeping matter to settle for next week. We have a witness to be called by Dr. Prlic's Defence, and they asked four hours for the examination-in-chief. I note that this witness testified already in the Naletilic case. So I wonder, do you need four hours since we have already heard this witness? At least he was heard one day during the Naletilic trial. Do you really need four hours, Mr. Karnavas, for your first witness next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I do, Mr. President. Good afternoon, everyone. We'll try to keep it to three hours, but I don't want to promise something that I cannot deliver, but I think our assessment was somewhere between three and four. We'll try to move rather quickly. I trust since was -- he testified before, the Prosecution knows -- the gentleman knows what he more or less has to say. Also, I should say in that particular case it was rather different -- it was a different subject and also a different Defence team with different practices and procedures. So next week's testimony, that witness ties in with the following week's, and we did hear rather extensive testimony from the Prosecution in promoting their joint criminal enterprise theory that the Government of Croatia, in fact, was -- aside from trying to annex, but in the process they were mistreating the Muslim refugees failed to provide adequate assistance, discriminated their education when they arrived, did not provide them with sufficient humanitarian facilities over there, did not give them adequate housing facilities, all of that. So this gentleman is going to rebut, at least in part, one of the Prosecution's witness. I don't know -- I can't remember whether she testified in open or in closed session -- open -- yeah, that was Ms. Krajsek. So basically it's to rebut her -- and in fact, at the end of the day I was planning on reading -- going over a couple of points to, again, alert the Prosecution as to what I might be going into so that next week we don't have the same objection that was raised earlier, and we want to make sure that the Prosecution is very well prepared so it doesn't cry foul as they did this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One change to the transcript. Page 27.734, line 27. The word in French "opposantes" should be changed to be "composantes." That was the problem that occurred yesterday in connection with Mr. Praljak when he spoke. We listened to the sound recording and I was right. I said "composantes" and not "opposantes." This being said, you may proceed, Mr. Karnavas, as far as housekeeping matters are concerned. I think we should only have 15 minutes for the next break so that we can finish in time. Thank you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to perfect my record from yesterday because of the heat of the exchanges and because of the time constraints, sometimes I tend to speak rather fast and maybe not completing my thoughts, and I wanted to make sure that when we had that sort of interesting exchange of ideas on testimony and evidence and whether the person should be an expert or not, I just wanted to make sure that I was clear in my presentation, especially when I indicated to one of the members of the Trial Chamber that they should raise their objection, and I meant -- I made that specifically because unless there is some sort of a decision from the Bench, if there is one of the members who outright rejects the admission of certain testimony for whatever reason, obviously we want to have a record. But I wanted to make sure that I was understood properly and in that context also tie in the concept of professional Judges. Now, if we were in front of a jury, of course, I would be entitled to make my record outside the presence of the jury in order to have a record. Now, because we have professional Judges, we don't need to excuse anybody because it's axiomatic that the professional Judges can hear all of the testimony even if they think that perhaps the testimony is inadmissible, but at least it allows the party to make a full and complete record. Otherwise, for instance, on appeal, let's just say on appeal I wish to appeal a point on the grounds that perhaps there was a abuse of discretion by the Trial Chamber in disallowing certain evidence to come in, it would be very difficult for me to show that there was an abuse of discretion if, for instance, the Appeals Chamber didn't have in front of it the information of which I was trying to elicit from the witness, and they could concretely, the Appeals Chamber could concretely say, Well, I think the Judges should have accepted this testimony or not. So the practice would be, for instance, and again I want to go to the Anglo-Saxon system where you have a jury to make the point very clear. If I object and the Judge says, for instance, I will disallow this testimony, and then I don't have a record from the witness as to what that witness would have said, in other words, what the jurors would have heard because they are the triers of fact, then I have failed in my job because I have not perfected my record, and clearly, the Appeals Chamber cannot do anything because there is no record from which to appeal. So yesterday when I indicated that I -- we should hear the gentleman and that we have professional Judges, it was in that context, in other words, that -- that I make a record. If, however, there is one particular member of the Bench who feels categorically prior to hearing all of the evidence because we do have the civil law system when it comes to the introduction of evidence, in a sense we get to hear all the evidence and the end you get to decide how much weight if any you will give to it. Even when it's hearsay, we get it in. Even when there's a lack of foundation, for instance, you may hear it. You may decide later on not -- to disregard it, but those are the rules that we have been operating under. If, however, there is a particular member of the Bench who strongly feels for whatever reason that this witness is not qualified, not competent to answer certain questions, then, one, I should be allowed to at least ask those questions to make a record, but two and more importantly, I would like categorically for that answer from the Judge to be on the record that under no circumstances they will consider this, so at least later on I can say if it is necessary that there was an abuse of judicial discretion in considering this piece of evidence and, in fact, maybe even go so far as to say that there was a pre-judgement. What I failed to say and what I should have been said yesterday was also one other point, which might have been more important for the exchange that I had with Judge Trechsel because I think I failed in articulating my point in that sometimes there's follow-up evidence that will establish the basis for which he's able to give insight into the evidence of which I'm trying to elicit at the moment. In this case, it was a transcript from 1991 - he wasn't present - the content of which he might be able to -- I might be able to show subject to connection, because of other events and what have you, that he is, in fact, capable of providing insight. As to whether you wish to accept that insight, that's another story. But I should have articulated it more clearly, and that is that perhaps we should allow the witness to provide answers to those questions, subject to connection. In other words, if I can connect it later on that he has the foundation to give insight that at least it merits consideration, and then again you would consider to what extent to give it that -- to give what weight to it. So I want to make sure that we're clear on what I was trying to establish. I'm not complaining in any way. I just want to make sure that we're on the same level. Now, in keeping with all of this because of these presidential transcripts especially, there was a prior decision that indicated that we would be able to introduce them during our case, and in order to facilitate the rest of the trial and not waste time on these matters, I would request that we have some sort of a 65 ter hearing with the Judges and the Legal Officers so we don't take up valuable courtroom time so we can have -- exchange these ideas. We can have an exchange of ideas and maybe come up with some solutions or conclusions so we can save the time so I don't have to make my objections and Mr. Scott or whoever it is from that side take time and respond and what have you. So I just wanted to make those points rather very clear because we want to make sure that we have our record, we have our record. And so I didn't mean any disrespect, Judge Trechsel. When I said, you know, for you to register your objection, that's what I was trying to convey at the time. So that's the one point that I wanted to make. The second point I wanted to make is -- which is something different has to do with evidence -- with the evidence that the other Defence teams intend to use in the -- during this phase of the case. It was my understanding that as of the 31st of March, the Defence teams were to download into the e-court system their documents so others would have access to them. In other words, not merely providing the list but also downloading the documents. That has not been done by all, and I just want some clarification. What is the rule? Because I'm entitled to re-direct, and I shouldn't be in a position where I'm in the dark even because I wanted to make sure that we all understand, we're not in some joint criminal enterprise on this side. I don't know what these folks are doing. I don't know what their defences are. In fact, from one team today, I don't even know what their documents are because I haven't seen them, and so I would ask for a ruling on that, what is the procedure, because it appears to me from what I've heard the Prosecutor was provided with a CD of the documents but our Defence has not. Now, why the Petkovic team did that, I don't know, but I certainly would like an explanation as to what the procedure is because if it's within their right to withhold that, that's fine; if not, I would like it disclosed immediately. That's the ... And then the third point -- part that I wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I don't want to interrupt or intervene in problems that may occur between the Defence teams, but the second issue you've just addressed could have been dealt with if you and your other colleagues had met and had asked the Petkovic Defence how it was that they would send a CD to the Prosecution and would fail to send you a copy thereof, and you should have settled that between, among, yourselves. But you're right in raising the issue as far as I can see, and this is my own personal opinion. When I speak I speak on my own behalf and not on behalf of the other Judges. As far as I can see, it's only normal when a Defence team makes up a list of their exhibits, then everybody should be informed, everybody, including the other Defence team. That's the least you can do. But as far as the second issue, you can easily settle it among yourselves. I believe that Ms. Alaburic is going to do so because she wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before she does that, we did ask for the list for today, for instance. We did ask quite politely, quite early, so we could see, and we got what is commonly known as the bum's rush: Wait until you finish your direct, we'll give you. Now, that gives me a certain message. Now, we've been waiting for weeks. We've asked others. Others have provided it, so I'm not in a position to negotiate. I won't negotiate. I want to know what the rules are, and I expect my colleagues to abide by the rules the very way the Prosecution in the Prlic Defence has to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you say, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, good afternoon to you and good afternoon to everyone else in the courtroom. I would like to say the following. I really have no idea what sort of request or demand Mr. Karnavas is talking about. This is the very first I hear of a list of exhibits that was requested by him from my Defence or anyone else. As for the CD with General Petkovic's Defence documents, which is something that was handed over to the OTP, we only acted pursuant to a ruling by this Court. By the 31st of March, we were supposed to hand in our 65 ter (g) list, and the OTP was supposed to forward documents, and we were supposed to forward hard copies of those documents to the Trial Chamber. The Petkovic Defence team acted entirely in keeping with the Court's ruling. The ruling never says that we have to do these documents in e-court. The fact that we have not done that so far has a purely technical explanation. It is over the last couple of days that we've been working on releasing all our documents into the e-court system. Furthermore, as for the documents to be used by General Petkovic's Defence in our cross-examination of today's witness, I wish to remind my colleague Mr. Karnavas about his own actions and about the actions taken by all of the Defence teams when the Prosecution witnesses were being cross-examined. We never provided lists of documents that we were using to the OTP ahead of time, no sort of list at all before a witness was heard; rather, we handed over to the OTP documents that we were going to use before the very start of our cross-examination. Documents that I will be using today have been prepared. They will be delivered to Mr. Karnavas in much the same way as was the case when the -- during the Prosecution case. Should the Trial Chamber make a different ruling as regards the time that these documents are handed over to be used in our cross-examination, the Petkovic Defence team will abide by any such decision. Therefore, this is no discrimination whatsoever, no refusal to hand over documents. All I'm talking about is we are applying the same treatment now we previously applied to the OTP when we cross-examined their witnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We understand the problem. We are going to discuss it among ourselves. Let's go back to the first issue discussed by Mr. Karnavas, and my fellow Judge is going to answer, but as the presiding judge, I'm going to say something that is only on my behalf. As to the discussion held yesterday and today, it's a bit of a storm in a teacup. The main thing is not to know whether the testimony of one expert is more relevant than the testimony of an ordinary witness. That's not the issue. The issue is simply this: In what an expert, what an ordinary witness says, what is important for the parties is -- parties' cases. The fact that you are an expert does not necessarily mean that what you say is more relevant than what an ordinary witness says. I said that yesterday. In matters of foreign affairs, in international public law, in international negotiations, if you have a simple witness who happens to have been minister of foreign affairs of his country, who happens to have participated in all relevant international negotiations, I think that what he says may be important, may be as relevant as what an expert would say. That's what I wanted to say at this stage. It's not a problem at all for me. I think all this time would have been better used if questions had been put to the witness, but my fellow Judge wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not only changing the language, but my approach is not exactly the same. As you are well aware, I come from a different legal system, and I have good news and bad news for you. First, bad news, perhaps. In our system and our conceptions, there are witnesses and there are experts and they are not the same. There are rules that apply to experts and rules that apply to witnesses, and I started on the assumption that it was the same here. Witnesses tell what they have seen, heard, smelt, you name it. You have often yourselves given the list to the witness. Experts are first tested as to their competencies. You do that very harshly. I'm glad that I'm not an expert here -- well, no, I don't think I would be really afraid, but you know what I mean. And experts give opinions. Now, you have asked in my view questions that were expert questions, and that's why I intervened, and there is still a difference of opinion maybe. That's the bad part. Now comes the good part. Contrary to the American, in particular, system, our system does not have an exclusionary rule, so that I am not here having my notes and crossing out entire pages by saying, this in my view is not admissible. I would like this -- these proceedings to go in strict respect of the rules, but I am not exclusionary-minded. Now, you've suggested a Rule 65 ter conference. That, of course, is not for me as one member of this Chamber to answer. The Chamber will certainly take that into account and give you an answer, which the President then will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but not for the Prosecution to be left out, but my comment will be very, very short, and I do want to pick up on what Judge Trechsel said. Just so the record is clear, Mr. Karnavas is always very active about wanting to make his record, and just so the Prosecution's view is also on the record. We stand by, I stand by, we stand by the comment that I made yesterday. This is nonetheless maybe a different system, indeed, a different system than the American or English common-law system, but it is a system, and inherent in a system is a system has rules. And there are rules for both the parties, the lawyers, and for the Judges, and for the Judges, to follow and respect. Otherwise, Your Honours, we wouldn't need this rule book. We would just have one rule, and you would open the book, and we'd turn to the first page, and rule one would say, everything goes, everything goes, and that's not the procedure, that's not the system we operate in. There are procedural rules, evidentiary rules, for the parties and the Judges to abide by. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the rules for the Judges, you say, could you specify them? Could you tell us to what extent the Judges would fail to comply with the Rules? I'm rather surprised .

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The rules are in this book, Your Honour. I'm sure the Chamber knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I won't reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Zuzul, we left off with our conversation concerning various issues that you had been involved with. I want to turn now to document -- I believe it's 1D 00397, and just very quickly, we see on the third page, at the top of the page, it has 128. It says: "Statement by Dr. Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia." If we look at the bottom, it was delivered on the 26th of August, 1992, at the London Conference. First question: Were you at the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was visiting China in my official capacity at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time, were you stationed in Geneva, or were you still working in Zagreb and closely associated with Dr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was the deputy foreign minister, and I was based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Have you had an opportunity to review this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to speed things up today a little bit because we need to cover a lot of ground, in the very first page Dr. Tudjman talks about his dissatisfaction with the response of the international community in trying to find a solution concerning the ongoing aggression against Croatia. Was that the case at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Nothing was changing for the better. Much of Croatia's territory was still occupied, and there were no signs that the international community would be doing anything to change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to read one passage, the bottom of the first page going into the next page, and ask you to comment on this. It says: "The Republic of Croatia had spared no efforts in order to prevent the escalation of the state and political crisis in the former Yugoslavia into an armed conflict. Accordingly, Croatia proposed the transformation of the former state into a confederal association of sovereign states. When this proposal was turned down and when war ensued, Croatia agreed to the peaceful solution by accepting the Vance Plans." Now, the first day that you testified, you talked about a confederation, and you talked about the presidents going around meeting with each other. Is that what President Tudjman is talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. President Tudjman is referring to his own proposal for Yugoslavia to be transformed into a confederal union of sovereign states, among other things, as he points out in order to avoid a war or an aggression which he saw coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the third paragraph on this page he talks about -- he says, the relevant part: "It should be noted that the Republic of Croatia in the area of Slovonski Brod Zupanja is continuously being attacked from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Was that the case at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where exactly is Slovonski Brod Zupanja?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear Mr. Zuzul.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Zuzul, if you would sit down, and I apologize for not having handy the number of the document -- the chart that you're pointing to for the record, and we'll get to that in a second, but first could you just tell us exactly what's that area called?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this is the Posavina area. One of its parts is in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other in Croatia around the river Sava. The Serb forces at the time still believed they were able to achieve their primary aim and create a line stretching from Karlobag to Virovitica. They were carrying out severe attacks from Bosnia and Herzegovina. THE INTERPRETER. [Previous translation continues] ... wait before he answers because he's not listening to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You're going to have to slow down a little bit. I know you were pointing at the map, and I apologise for the Court because for the record I'm unable to identify it at this moment, but I think we all know what area Mr. Zuzul is talking about. Incidentally -- and this is 3171 for identification purposes. Now, that area, when was it finally liberated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It is only a technical matter. I'm sorry to interrupt -- for interrupting you. The interpreter is asking you, Mr. Zuzul, to be kind enough to use your earphone and to listen to them because otherwise you cannot communicate with each other. So kindly use the -- actually what the interpreters are saying and listen to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to help you out, Mr. Zuzul, 4 is English; 6 is Croatian or B/C/S, I believe, the channel, so there's a channel here so if you want to hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And channel 5 for French.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could wait, if you could pause a little bit. I'm getting all these instructions here, sort of like cross by committee. But anyway, going back to my earlier question, when was that area liberated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I apologise, Mr. Karnavas, I have confusion if I'm listening myself and talking at the same time, so can I speak without having speakers in my -- I apologise. I'm trying to be concentrated to the maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The idea is, of course, not that you listen to yourself in direct but that you listen to the sound of the interpretation, and you can turn the volume low so that it is not too disturbing, but if you do that, then you get a feeling of whether you are too fast or not, and then you can slow down, and you sense that the interpreters lose thread. It is a bit annoying. We quite understand that, but it's not the pleasure trip to be a witness here, anyhow. I'm sorry. You may have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to make it as pleasant as possible, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just wait for cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go into the next page, page 130, towards the latter part of the page, it gives certain numbers of refugees and displaced persons. And it says "Croatia still has more than 270.000 persons displaced from various Croatian regions while an additional number of more than 80.000 are being provided relief in other countries: Hungary, Austria, Germany, Switzerland." And then it goes on to say "More than 400.000 refugees have fled to Croatia from Bosnia and Herzegovina together with an additional 35.000 Croatian refugees that have come from Vojvodina and Kosovo." Now, one quick question: Is this more or less accurate, what President Tudjman is saying at the London Conference as far as the numbers of displaced persons, that Croatia was generating within itself and, of course, the refugees that were fleeing from its neighbour, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The figures are certainly accurate. This is a sad picture of the truth as it was at the time. Nearly 8.000 [as interpreted] people were forced to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And one last point to make sure that I didn't forget. When President Tudjman was saying --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] There is mistake in translation. It says nearly 8.000. I said nearly 800.000 people were forced to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when President Tudjman is saying that Croatia is being attacked from Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that truthful? Was that happening at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to the next document, 1D 01935, and we can see at the top of it, it says: "The president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, proceeding from the Agreement of Friendship and Cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia on 21 July and" -- I underscore that for everyone's attention -- "following talks between the delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia which were held on 21 September 1992 in New York during the 47th Session of the General Assembly of the United Nations." Before I go on, let me ask you this question: This Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation, is that what we talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go on to the next page because -- and I mention that because this was the part where we talked where the Prosecution was alleging that Izetbegovic had been pressed to enter into this agreement. It seems now, a few weeks later, here we have an annex to that agreement, which says: "The diplomatic, political, and humanitarian efforts of the international community has so far failed to stop the aggression." Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see it's both for Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. If we go to number 2, it talks about equal and integral community of three constituent peoples, that is in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What exactly was meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was meant was the key thread that runs through all these rounds of negotiations. For centuries in Bosnia, there were three ethnic groups, all equal, and here they were termed constituent. The term was used deliberately here in order to point out their equality, regardless of their respective sizes, which is something that changed over time. Their constituent status and their equal rights before the law were values to be preserved at all costs. This was a given and something that President Tudjman always advocated, and I think the same goes for the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was an ongoing position. It was an ongoing request, and this was something that never changed over the course of the negotiations. However, we see that the international community used the same phrasing. From the very beginning, each of the peace agreements talked about the constituent nature and character of all three ethnic groups. I could provide further comments as to why that was particularly important, if you would like me to. However, we may be coming to that at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's just do that now so that when we get to it we can breeze through it because I think it might be important, although by now it should be rather obvious to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, I will try to sum up the respective positions of the three ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the negotiations. Negotiations normally result in some sort of compromise. That is normally the case, but if we look at their course in this case, the position of the Serb party was continually to grab as much territory as possible and keep it. Throughout the course of the negotiations, they were always adamant that whatever they had been successful in seizing they should keep. The position of the Muslim side, and then there was a name change, and they became the Bosniak side, and I do think that this is a very fair interpretation of all the documents and all the situations, was this: They wanted to set up a state that would be as unitary as possible. Unitary in which sense? More often than not, it was formulated by the Bosniaks as follows: Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state should be set up on the following principle: One man/one vote. This is one of the existing democratic models for organizing states, but this would have severely impinged on the constituent nature of all the three ethnic groups. The Muslims and Bosniaks were the most numerous, and they would end up with an overwhelming majority. This is not something that is peculiar to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most contemporary states are organized along federal lines in order to avoid one particular group ending up with an overwhelming majority in terms of sheer numbers or in terms of territory. Likewise, we see that throughout, the Croats were the smallest group and the group most at risk. Were this principle now to be abandoned and were the unitary principle to be adopted, the Croats would be left facing the most difficult situation of all by a long chalk. That is why the principal departure point in all of the negotiations and I would say the bottom line as far as the Croatian negotiators were concerned was to keep all of the three ethnic groups as constituents. This principle was to be preserved at all costs. I can tell you that all the peace plans, Cutileiro's peace plan, Vance-Owen, Vance-Stoltenberg, the Washington Agreement, the Dayton Accords, if you look at any of those, they all take that as their departure point. They all recognise the necessity regardless of how the community would be organized to take into account the constituent nature of all three ethnic groups. This was the only way in which their equality as well as their survival could be safe-guarded and guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for that very complete answer. We won't have to touch on that again. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have a certain knowledge. You have some particular skills, and as such you can help the Judges, the triers of fact, to understand the matters they are seized of, and I'm thinking of the definition given in the Galic case on the 3rd of July, 2002, regarding two experts, Tabeau and someone else. You are perfectly able to answer a number of questions for us. You've just explained that the existence of these three ethnic groups was taken into account in the international negotiations as far as the Dayton, the Washington, and the Cutileiro agreements or plans. But what about the constitution of your own country? In Croatia, are these -- is this component of these three ethnic groups included in the constitution of your own country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was very much taken into account, and I think the issue was dealt with in keeping with the highest possible standards of modern democracy. However, the Republic of Croatia is not a federal state. There was no reason for that simply because none of the other ethnic groups in Croatia could enjoy a constituent status such as that enjoyed by the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were different solutions, and those were referred to in the preamble to the Croatian constitution. We've been looking at that, and I believe a copy somewhere among our documents. There were several solutions. For example, all of the minorities were guaranteed a seat in the Croatian parliament, a total of eight. Three of those went to the Serb ethnic minority; however, they remain ethnic minorities, and that is their status. They are not constituent groups. These are differences of both fact and history and differences in terms of how a state was first created. Bosnia and Herzegovina was always a country that belonged to three different ethnic groups. Ever since the Ottomans left, it was clear who was left, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was their only home. I'm of course referring to the three ethnic groups that are here and rightly so, I believe, defined as the three constituent peoples. I don't believe that anyone in all earnestness ever tried to draw a parallel during the negotiations between Croatia's constitution and Bosnia and Herzegovina's constitution. When models were considered and one had to pick a model to be used in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the models that were studied were those belonging to countries with a comparable past or with a comparable situation. At one point in time, Belgium's model was considered. It's difficult for me to discuss which model is good and which was not, but at one point in time, serious consideration was given to Switzerland's model. We spoke about a possible cantonisation, about ten cantons along which Bosnia and Herzegovina would be organized, but even so, the three ethnic groups would all remain constituent. At one point in time, one considered seriously the constitution of the United States of America. The international community, as well, was considering all these models, and so were the negotiating teams. The question being asked was: What were the models of democracy in our modern world, and what was the model that would best fit these constituent peoples, and what would be the best guarantee for their equal rights without necessarily being at the expense of the appropriate functioning of the state or the country itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zuzul, and for Your Honours, if you turn to the very first document, which was 1D 2039, we don't need to do that, but if you do turn to it on page 2, the answer lies there where it talks about the Croatian -- the Republic of Croatia being -- having been established as the national state of the Croatian people and a state of members of other nations and minorities, and I believe Mr. [Indiscernible] helped us with that. But we'll be getting into that a little bit more, too, with one of our other witnesses. If we stick with this document now, on paragraph 3 it talks about: "In keeping with the right to self-defence and to joint defence from aggression, a joint committee will be set up in order to harmonize defence efforts until the aggression stops completely." What was meant by that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an elaboration of what was already envisaged in the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation. It is important to note here that this document was signed in New York. Both presidents attended the General Assembly of the United Nations. I was a member of our delegation, and if I'm not mistaken - and I don't think that I am - I actually worked on this document. This paragraph is an expression of the awareness on the part of both presidents that unfortunately the Yugoslav aggression, or rather, the aggression by the Yugoslav People's Army or the Serbian army had not been stopped, and in a way there is this feeling of disappointment engendered by the knowledge that the international community would fail to put a stop to this aggression any time soon, and that the only way to defend the country was to mount a joint defence. I think that this is just making some items that were already signed and agreed to in the Agreement on Cooperation and Friendship more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I think if we look at the next paragraph, and I think this may be of some importance to complete your answer. "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will jointly seek the lifting of the embargo on the import of arms into the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia." Can you tell us a little bit about that, and why was it important to lift the embargo? Because, I mean, the Prosecution's theory as we all know is that there was this joint criminal enterprise, and here it appears that both are seeking the lifting of an embargo for arms to be going into Bosnia and Herzegovina presumably to arm the Muslims for the ongoing aggression that was all over the country and from Bosnia towards the Republic of Croatia. So can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how Croatia or, indeed, Bosnia and Herzegovina got their weapons. What I do know is that they did manage to obtain weapons because, after all, they managed to defend themselves in the war. I know what avenues were close to them for obtaining weapons. They could not -- unlike the majority of the states that were members of the United Nations, they could not simply procure those weapons officially because at the beginning of the Yugoslav aggression an embargo, an arms embargo, was imposed, and applying some sort of weird logic, it applied to all the parts of the former Yugoslavia. Why do I say that it's weird logic? Because at that time one, or rather, two republics, Serbia and Montenegro, kept all the weapons that had been in the possession of the Yugoslav People's Army. But not only that, even the weapons that existed in the republics, that were held by the so-called Territorial Defence, had been seized by the Yugoslav institutions, so that when the war broke out there were three facts that we had to take into consideration. On the one hand, an extremely well-armed military. Some people speculated that it was among the best-equipped armies in Europe. History has shown that not to be the case, but be that as it may, they were very well armed. We had the other republics, first Slovenia, then Croatia, and finally Bosnia and Herzegovina, that did not have their own military. They did not have these kind of weapons. What little weapons they had under the Territorial Defence system had already been seized. And there is the third fact, unfortunately, and that is the fact that the international community decided to impose an embargo, an arms embargo, that applied across the board to everyone, even those who had no need of importing weapons - that would be the Yugoslav People's Army - and to those who really needed those weapons to defend themselves. That is why at this point - this was a topic that frequently cropped up - the two presidents seek the support of the international community to lift the embargo. I can say, and this will become evident from further transcripts, that we had a lively diplomatic activity in this regard. But unfortunately, at that time, this time that we're now talking about, there was no will to change this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's move on to the next document, 1D 01540, and this is from the Security Council. You'll see it's dated 2 October 1992, and I just wanted to -- very brief comments. From the very first page, it says: "Dr. Franjo Tudjman and the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic, that they had met on 30th September, 1992." Are you -- did that, in fact, occur ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would seem -- it seems from looking at this document, does it not, that this meeting was at the behest and with the encouragement of the international community, that is, those who were involved in the negotiating process at the time, Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and just if we go to the very first paragraph, it says, number one: "The two presidents re-affirm the commitment of the international conference in London on the inviability [Realtime transcript read in error "viability"] of existing borders other than through changes reached by peaceful agreement." And that statement there, did that include the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, since at that time Bosnia and Herzegovina was an internationally recognised country within its borders, existing borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this rather changes the sense. In the transcript it says the viability of existing borders, page 26, line 7, and I think inviability would be the right word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, I agree, I agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm reading a bit fast and it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go into the next document 1541. These are all sort of interconnected. Here we see this again is dated 21 October 1992, and it appears on the very first page we have Mr. Dobrica Cosic with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, that there was a meeting on 20th October in Geneva. And if we look at the annex, and if you look at paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 very quickly, does it not give the appearance that this is a very similar document only this time it's between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is indeed a similar document. The co-chairmen encouraged and set up meetings between the presidents, and if I may just note -- draw your attention to a very important difference between the two documents. In the first document, paragraph 3, if I'm not mistaken, it is stated that the Yugoslav Army would leave Prevlaka by the 20th of October. Why do I say that? Because yesterday and the day before yesterday we spoke at length about the aggression by the Yugoslav Army on the area of Prevlaka and Dubrovnik. That's the area that we were talking about. So here, the Yugoslav president admits that this area was occupied by the Yugoslav Army, and he undertakes that by the 20th of October the army would pull out. Of course, it never happened. After the 20th of October, the attacks escalated, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that document that you were referring to is, for example, 1D 01540. Now, if you could go on to 1D 01542, we see that this is from the General Assembly, Security Council, looks like, 22 October 1992, and from the very first page we see that this is something between Cosic and Dr. Franjo Tudjman. And if we look at the annex, it says here that there was a -- it appears that there was some sort of a meeting in Geneva, 20 October, and the paragraph that I'm most interested in is paragraph 6 where it says: "The two presidents re-affirmed their determination to exert all of their influence toward a just, peaceful solution in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They urge all parties to the conflict to direct all necessary efforts toward a cessation of hostilities and the negotiations of a constitutional arrangement for Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of the agreement between the three constituent peoples." So we come back to that thesis. Now, the reason I'm asking for this is I have one question: Was it President Tudjman and maybe Mr. Cosic that were maybe sort of approaching the UN and the internationals to get engaged in the process, or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document states quite clearly that the meeting was held under the auspices of the co-chairmen, Messrs. Vance and Owen, so the international community organized such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Help me out here. Did the international community ever ask Dr. Tudjman to engage in a particular meeting, to sit down with someone, and he refused? Be it Karadzic, be it Milosevic, be it Cosic, be it someone else? To your knowledge, that is, did he ever refuse to sit down, to meet, to ratify some sort of a negotiated solution to this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such case. Whenever there was an official invitation sent through me as the ambassador or in any other capacity, President Tudjman responded, agreeing to come. But I often heard President Tudjman say -- after all, he was sometimes criticised by the Croatian media for negotiating, for instance, with Milosevic when it was quite obvious that Milosevic was the one perpetrating the aggression. He was in a position to give a simple answer, that's what the international community is asking me to do, and that answer would have been both simple and accurate. But in most cases, he would say, I would negotiate with the blackest devil if it would then result in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01543, this is 2 November 1992. This is a joint communique on the president -- on the talks between the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic dated 1 November 1992. And if we look at the annex, we look at it, and we see the second paragraph, they say -- it says to the effect: They reviewed the implementation of the Friendship And Cooperation Agreement between the two countries and discussed a number of topical issues of mutual interest, especially the recent misunderstandings. This may go in to answer the President's question yesterday as far as whether the international community was aware of this. But are we talking about the Friendship and Cooperation Agreement that we talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that at least everybody is aware of it, that these two countries are trying to cooperate against a common aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it goes on to say that: "President Izetbegovic informed President Tudjman that next week Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to appoint its ambassador to Zagreb." Now, did they eventually appoint an ambassador to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was just as announced here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did Croatia -- did President Tudjman appoint an ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's -- if we go on to the next paragraph: "The two presidents agreed that the latest conflict between some BH army units and the Croatian Defence Council HVO formations were detrimental to their continued struggle against the joint aggressor. These conflicts should be stopped immediately and the culprits dismissed and punished." And then it says that: "A joint unbiassed commission will be set up to determine individual responsibility. Similar occurrences will be avoided in the future through proper actions involving urgent formation -- including urgent formation of a joint command of armed forces of BH and HVO." Now, to your knowledge, why was it necessary to have this part, to agree to this? I mean, why is Izetbegovic -- or Tudjman, I should say, discussing this matter with Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the field was as follows: The aggression by the Serb forces was ongoing. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council were now mounting a joint defence. I cannot really interpret the events in the field because I was working at the diplomatic level, but it is quite obvious that for various reasons there were some sporadic incidents that are mentioned here at some points in time. The presidents were now trying to find a way to avoid such incidents, ways in which an efficient defence could be mounted, and were trying to see how those two armies could become as well integrated as possible in accordance with the agreement in order to be able to defend the country successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sure. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For some reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Now, Mr. Zuzul, the passage you have been pointed to speaks of the fact that: "The culprits must be dismissed and punished ..." Can you see it? It's really in the middle of the first page of the document. Do you know whether any action followed this declaration on either side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of actions in general terms, but I was not really familiar with the specific situations encountered in the implementation on the ground. This was not something that I was dealing with. I think that action was taken, but I cannot say what action, when, and what the results were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go on to the next document, 1D 01312. This is 11 November 1992, and have you had a chance to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And because we're running out of time, I see if we look at the contents under number 4 it talks about working groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then we see under number 7, second page, working group on succession issues, number 9, working group on confidence and security building and verification measures. And then we have a series of annexes, and in the annexes -- so we see, for instance, number 2, the joint declaration issued at Geneva, 30 September 1992, and then on, say, number 6 we have the joint declaration issued on 20th October. We see Tudjman named now -- this is what we have been talking about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is the document stipulating the manner in which the conference on the former Yugoslavia in Geneva would work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll move on to the next document, and that would be P 00854. This is 3 December 1992, and from the contents we see in number 4, withdraw on foreign forces, which would be on page 3, if we just turn to page 3 and 4, but I'm mostly interested in page 4, paragraphs 10 and 11, 10 and 11. Because it says in the middle of page -- of paragraph 10, it says: "The Bosnian Serb forces allegedly continued to receive supplies and support from elements of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" -- and that is Serbia and Montenegro -- "There are also journalistic accounts of foreign nationals fighting alongside, alongside, Muslim and Croat forces." And then if we go to number 11, paragraph number 11: "The JNA has withdrawn completely from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Former members of Bosnian Serb origin have been left behind with their equipment and constitute the 'army of the Serb republic.' Several brigades of the Croatian army are also reliably reported to be actively engaged in the conflict. This provision of the General Assembly resolution, also, therefore, appears not to have been fulfilled." And so, could you comment on that a little bit because it would appear that, yes, you have the Yugoslav forces still there, albeit having a different uniform but basically using the same equipment and same manpower, but also we see that there are references to the -- to the elements of the Croatian army. And in answering that question, I would ask you: Has the situation changed at all; that is, is Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, territory of it, that is, still being attacked by the JNA, by the Serb forces, from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Croatia was still under attack from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in various areas but most of all in the Dubrovnik area. We're talking about the same time-frame we discussed at length yesterday, I think. This report of the Secretary-General shows quite clearly that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian forces are fighting side by side. They're fighting a common enemy. It is quite clear from the text as a whole and specifically from paragraph 10. We thought at the time, and it is still the case -- it still seems so to me, that this was in line with the Agreement on Friendship and with the two annexes of the implementation of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I may add, this sentence in the reports by foreign journalists about foreigners fighting in the ranks of Muslims and Croats, at that time first reports were published about the Mujahedin units fighting side by side with Muslims, Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, P 00890. This is a presidential transcript dated 10 December 1992. P 00890, and as I understand it, you were present during this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you one question when you -- the first day you testified because you mentioned someone by the name of Biscevic, who's also featured in this particular transcript. Just to make sure that we have one minor detail nailed down, you indicated that he had been Croatia's ambassador to Turkey at one point, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at one point he had -- President Tudjman had asked you to bring him along to assist you in some negotiations where, I believe, it was Komsic from Sarajevo was attending; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Biscevic, as I understand it at the time, he was a Croatian but he was Muslim; is that correct? Muslim I guess by way of religion, not to distinguish -- to make the distinguish -- to distinguish it from, say, a Bosniak or a Muslim from Bosnia-Herzegovina as a constituent people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Ambassador Biscevic quite well. I don't know what his faith is because we didn't really discuss that, but it is quite true that he is of Muslim origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this particular transcript, I wanted to just focus you on something, and perhaps you can provide us with some insight because you were there. On page 41, we have the president speaking. He begins speaking, and there's a long exchange, but again, because of the time constraints we'll have to cut it short. And if we go to page 42, the second-to-last paragraph where it says -- it starts with: "Let's face the situation. The issue is not just Croat/Serb antagonism in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's not just the problem of Muslims within that; rather, it is the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the conflict of the Western world with the Islamic world. That was the path between the devil and the deep blue sea that we had to pass and why Europe and the Western world allowed the aggression of Serbia on -- such aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina we have been witnessing to this very day. Why did it then try to transfer the blame on us for its action in that? However, we have come out of it, so with this thing that the Western world had to thrust aside the attempt of transferring the blame on us, remember what -- it wasn't even two or three months when they asked a question even the sanction against Croatia, wasn't it? So they had to throw away that idea. On the other hand, the Islamic world also had to accept the fact that we had been the ones who recognised Bosnia and who accepted, et cetera, et cetera. Thus, in both the Western and the Islamic worlds, in the most delicate for us, this gap, this situation we have managed to establish ourselves through our consistency. That is something that seemed to me as squaring the circle from the very beginning." But then he goes on to say: "But it's clear, that's the truth. That's truth, and we have to be aware of it, for it is true that Izetbegovic and his were not fundamentalists in the sense how to -- how to spread, and I don't know what -- but they wanted an Islamic state, and it's true that they, not only moderate Muslim states like Turkey and Egypt but also Iran and others, wanted through him to stir up trouble in the area of Europe within this conflict between Iran and Islamic fundamentalists in the West." Can you tell us what exactly is President Tudjman talking about? Because in that very first transcript that we talked about yesterday, there were references to Iran, and of course you now have spent quite a bit of time with Tudjman, and you see the issue of Iran again at some point. So can you help us out here since you were one of the insiders?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to sum this up in just a couple of words. What is President Tudjman doing here? He's drawing some sort of a conclusion. He's summing up and commenting on reports that were submitted to him at this meeting. If you read the transcript, you will see that this is about foreign policies. The main body of the report is a report submitted by the then foreign minister Mr. Skrabalo, who along with Mr. Biscevic visited several Muslim states to talk specifically about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and generally about Croatia's relations to both the Islamic and non-Islamic worlds. I can say that this was something that Tudjman was very mindful of. It was right after this meeting that I as deputy for the minister was tasked with visiting a number of other Islamic centuries, as a matter of fact, nearly all of those that remained after the first visits made by the minister, the objective being to talk about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what Croatia's role would be in that future, and how one could forestall an incursion by Islamic extremists into Europe through Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's difficult to be more specific than that, but I think President Tudjman was very mindful of that. May I just bring something else up. It was back in 1991, 1992, and 1993 that the issue of Islamic extremism came up throughout the world. If I'm not mistaken, Samuel Huntington right about this time published an article on the clash of civilizations in the Foreign Affairs magazine. The article caused a lot of stir and drew a number of emphatic reactions. President Tudjman always liked to consider things within the wider context of history as a whole, so this is precisely what we see him doing now. He's raising a question that, to be quite frank, I'd already heard raised by many prominent statesmen and thinkers, including Samuel Huntington himself. The question came down to this: Would Bosnia and Herzegovina now possibly be used as a gate for Islamic extremism to penetrate Europe? This is in global terms. He talks about the consistency of his policies, and again, there is one thing that I can point out because this was a message that I and before minister Skrabalo and Mr. Biscevic had taken to Islamic countries. What was consistent about this was the fact that Croatia was prepared to abide by the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina was there; it was a neighbouring country. Croatia believed that it was necessary to have a friendship with Bosnia and Herzegovina; likewise, however, Croatia was adamant that it had to protect the interests of Croats within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... answer. I can see that Mr. Karnavas has taken a new binder. It may be time for the break because it's going to be 4.00 soon. Based on our count, you have another 30 minutes, Mr. Karnavas, so we're going to keep a close watch on you. After you, we're going to have cross-examination, but obviously enough, we are not going to have time to hear all the Defence counsel in their cross-examination. I don't know who's going to start. Is that you certainly, Ms. Alaburic? So she might be the only one today. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we didn't really coordinate this, but I suppose we'll be doing this in the usual order. The first Defence first. If Ms. Nozica has no cross-examination, as she said yesterday she might, then it will be General Praljak's Defence to start it off, and then I will pick up from there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, if you're not finished by 18:25, we'll continue in July next time. Anyway, we'll remember everything by then. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have about half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have, like, a 5-minute warning, as well, so I know. But I have stream-lined, so we won't go through all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured that I will warn you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I have no doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document, which would be 1D 02567, so we're skipping a couple, and we'll go to 1D 02567, and I'll ask you to just -- the next few documents are very quick. And you see that this is dated June 1, 1993, embassy of the Republic of BiH in the Republic of Croatia military economic office, and from the very start, it says: "On May 31, 1993, at approximately 0100 hours a.m., a group of total number of 19 fighters left the command district of the Slunj home guard regiment towards your command district. All of them are equipped and armed with equipment and weapons from warehouse of 5C." And then I think on the same document if we go to page number 4, we see -- after paragraph 19, we see: "In your command district there are six foreign nationals. Please enable the foreign national who is with this group to establish contact immediately with Mirsad Veladzic. And then, if we go to the very last page because this may be of some importance, we see that there is a stamp, and it says, military representative, office of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia, and then so on and so forth. And, of course, we've already talked yesterday or saw yesterday Avdic, who was then a president of the Presidency of BiH, at one point had come over asking to set up Main Staff in Rijeka and other offices. Can you opine as to what exactly is this document about? What does it demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you my interpretation of this document. I see the names of a group of fighters - they appear to be Muslims judging by their names - as well as a couple of foreigners. They were trained by the Slunj home guard regiment in Croatia's territory, after which they crossed to Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were trained, they were given weapons, and the weapons they were given are specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would this be a further demonstration of the Friendship and Cooperation Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that might be an accurate interpretation of the agreement, and this seems to be the materialisation of certain elements of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on -- now we're going to skip a couple -- a few documents, and we're going to go on to 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we just make clear to whom they are sending -- it says the 5th Corps. There are corps, of course, in all armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. We -- that's correct, and perhaps we should also see above, it says: "We are forwarding the report of the office of Bihac counties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's not the area of the indictment. It's the north-western corner of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. -- Your Honour. I guess what I'm trying to establish is that there is close cooperation between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's the essential part, and there was an agreement, and now we're seeing proof of the agreement, and also we see a date, June 1, 1993. And it goes into the greater context of the joint criminal enterprise to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I think this is the whole purpose of it, to show that we have these resolutions. The resolutions don't say exactly where these fighters are, but we see now that there's close cooperation. And so it also demonstrates -- I mean, President Tudjman, you know, has indicated over and over again that he is for a Bosnia and Herzegovina, contrary to the Prosecution's theory, and here's further demonstration. They've got Muslim fighters trained in Croatia, armed in Croatia, to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And once they get there, they're mobile. They can go wherever. You know, they can -- they can go to whatever front and shoot at anyone or kill anyone or maim anyone for that matter. But that was the purpose, and I hope this time wasn't taken off my 30 minutes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I know. All right. I just want to make sure that -- Mr. Registrar, sometimes seems that he doesn't turn off the timer. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, and it might also be of some assistance, Judge Trechsel, which is 1D 2573, again same variation, same theme. 1D 02573. Here we see that this is from the club Unski Ljiljani, Lilies of Una, and it's Zagreb, July 31, 1993, again, the date. And this is what it says: "Confirming that representatives of the Unski Ljiljani club from Munich handed 50.000 pieces of initial capsules of the office of the Bihac County in Zagreb for the need of the 5th Corps of BiH army that is active in the territory of Bihac region." Is this further verification of the implementation of the friendship agreement in your opinion, Mr. Zuzul?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this all falls within the framework of the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to skip the next document. We touched on it. The document that I wanted to discuss was 2896, and that had to do with the preliminary agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the parties of the constitutional agreement establishing the union of republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but just very briefly, having looked at this document, would this document be consistent with what you told us the first day as far as Croatia negotiating to provide a port to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, a port that would be used for commerce?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I think this document was prepared by the UN. This is even in the next document, the report of the co-chairmen to the secretary general, who brings up the idea of talking about the access to the sea being granted. This is also about the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its relations to the Republic of Croatia. Further, it is noteworthy that Bosnia and Herzegovina is here defined in no uncertain terms in what is known as a land-locked state in international law, a state, therefore, or a country that has no direct access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we go on to the next series of documents, they're kind of interconnected, 1D 01320, and with that we will discuss, also, just so everyone can cue into this, 1D 01321 and 3D 00451. They're sort of as a package, and we can see from 1D 01321 that this is from a text by Ivo Komsic, who, when, and where, divided BiH. Do you know Mr. Komsic, and very briefly, who is he, so I can go straight to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Komsic. I met him during the negotiations. He is a Croat from Bosnia. He sometimes appeared during the negotiations, and he had a number of different hats on during those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the document, we see that this is a joint declaration, September 14, 1993. It talks -- it's between Dr. Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic, accepting the principles of the London Conference, and if we look at paragraph number 5, it talks about establishing a working group for issues pertaining to the territorial division between the two republics in the envisaged union of BiH, including the issue of access to the sea as a joint development interest and so on. Very quickly, is this what you were talking about in the first day when you said that there had been a joint declaration signed by Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is the document that I spoke about the first day or yesterday. It's a document that was prepared by Mr. Biscevic and me on our side and Mr. Komsic and Mr. Silajdzic on behalf of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the next document 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, please. Witness, before we move on to the following document, I have a question about this particular document, the joint declaration by Tudjman and Izetbegovic dated September 14th, 1993. We can see here that you took part in this process because we see your name here. You have better knowledge of these type of issues than any other experts. At the beginning of this declaration, I see that reference is made to the London Conference, to the conference in Geneva, and I read: "On the constitutional system of the future union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the future union of republics." Talking about this concept of union of republics, was everybody aware of that in Geneva? Did everybody agree with that? Is this document in line with all the work conducted starting in London and in Geneva and including all the various plans? Was the union of these republics a part of a peace solution with access to sea, et cetera? Was the final objective the creation of the union of republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, the initiative for a meeting like this, an agreement like this, came from President Tudjman. He instructed me, and I promptly got in touch with Mr. Haris Silajdzic. President Tudjman believed that things were moving too slowly within the conference, and he believed that we should first consider the common interest of the Muslims and the Croats, which would then be used as a base for reaching some sort of an agreement, and that's why this meeting was organized. As I said, the four of us attended this meeting to discuss various possibilities. As you have just suggested, Mr. President, we used the plans proposed by the international community up to this point, and we took from them elements that we believed could be useful to building a future for Bosnia and Herzegovina. We tried to include all the key issues in order to arrive at a comprehensive proposal. We did, in fact, formulate a proposal. This is the proposal. It was signed by persons who at the time had the greatest political impact or influence, if you like, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. One thing, Mr. President, that I can add to this is that in addition to this document, on that same day, in fact, another document was signed that was believed to be a comprehensive solution to relations between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was also thought that it would guarantee stable relations in the region on a permanent basis. This was a document regarding a possible confederation between the Republic of Croatia and the Bosnia and Herzegovina union. It is not among these documents because it was agreed at the time that it would be kept secret. Although a mere three copies were made of the document, I think that it eventually surfaced somewhere. At any rate, I am quite familiar with the document. At the time, there was a lot of optimism and enthusiasm on both sides. I believe that all of us that were present - and this was a document that was signed at the Croatian mission in Geneva - believed at the time that we had just succeeded in resolving a major problem in an historical perspective. I can even go so far as to say that members of the Bosnian delegation, including Mr. Ganic, who was always the most critical and the most difficult negotiating partner, came to visit the building that housed our mission, asking themselves whether the building would be large enough to house both countries. This wasn't just a joke; they were actually raising issues of possible additions to the building. I think both we on the Croat side and the Muslims, too, for their part sincerely believed at the time that we had reached a solution. Unfortunately, as mentioned yesterday, a mere two days later, Mr. Izetbegovic signed an agreement with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's something else, something different, but I would like to relate this document to what the American ambassador in Zagreb told us, Mr. Galbraith. He came here a few months ago, and he told us that he would meet Tudjman on a daily basis - I'm paraphrasing what he told us - and my conviction was that the US embassy or the US ambassador was all the time at the Presidency in Zagreb. I'd like to know whether this joint declaration drafted in September 1993 had the agreement of the Americans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador Galbraith is a dear friend, to be quite frank. I am somewhat uncomfortable making comments on him like this, but I don't know [as interpreted] when it was that any of the ambassadors were meeting Tudjman. I don't think that there is even a theoretical possibility of an ambassador visiting Tudjman on a daily basis. There's one thing you must know.
