President Tudjman had a great respect for the United States, and that applied from the outset. He liked to talk to people; nevertheless, he was also a very formal person. He cared for formalities, and he respected issues of protocol. Communication between an ambassador and a state president is always a matter of protocol. It is easy enough to ascertain when and if such meetings took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister, of course I have nothing to teach you when it comes to protocol and visits and such-likes, but telephone exists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. I can't rule out the possibility that they occasionally spoke over the phone. However, based on as much as I know, Ambassador Galbraith didn't really discuss Bosnia and Herzegovina that much with President Tudjman. He was far more involved, if I may tell you my opinion, in bringing about a solution in Croatia, especially as concerned Eastern Slavonia. However, and I must be perfectly frank, I don't believe that he shared information about this agreement with anyone at the time the agreement was reached, nor do I believe that it was necessary at the time to inform him at all, as would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop here. I've heard enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a different question relating to the same document. In number 5, on top of the second page, there is mention of: "Establish a working group for issues pertaining to the territorial division between the two republics in the envisaged union of BiH." Could you specify what is meant with this territorial division that is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as can be seen if you look at the agreement, at the heading, at the course of the negotiations, this was supposed to be a union comprising republics, regardless of the fact that the republics were to be within a single community. One still needed to define their respective territories, which is always the case in any federal or confederal country. The territories of their respective federal units or republics must be defined, so that's what this was about: How to define each of the units' respective territories within the union. In the case of Croat-Muslim relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this wasn't always simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is an error in the transcript. I think it's quite material, otherwise I wouldn't be springing to my feet. Page 46, line 11, it reads: [In English] "uncomfortable making comments on him like this" -- it was about Ambassador Galbraith -- "but I don't know when it was that any of the ambassadors were meeting with Tudjman." Your Honours, I'm quite sure because I was listening on regional Croatian language and the transcript in English that actually the witness said "it would be easy to establish" instead of "but I don't know." He literally said: It would be easy to establish when it was that any of the ambassadors were meeting Tudjman. And I think this is the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right in the interpretation from B/C/S into French. This is exactly what I heard, so there must have been something that went wrong in the English transcript. Please proceed. Well, the time goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, this should count on your time, Mr. President, the next question because it was touched upon as a result of your question. If we go to 1D 01321.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You spoke about some sort of a secret agreement between, I believe -- I'm sorry. Let's look at the next document, and then we'll talk about this. It's 1D 01321. Here, it says: "Mr. President, in accordance with the joint declaration signed yesterday, I submit the names of our members of the agreed-upon working group." And then we see that this -- the next page is September 15, 1993, and if we look at the commentary at the bottom, which would have been from Mr. Komsic, the very last sentence, it says that: "Alongside this declaration that was drafted from several versions, another declaration was signed that wasn't made public and was kept only by Izetbegovic and Tudjman. This declaration contains provisions on maintaining the integrity of BiH, the alliance between Croats and Muslims, and the confederation between BiH and Croatia. When Tudjman spoke of a confederation, he had this declaration in mind." Now, first of all, do you know anything about this declaration that they're talking about, this version of the declaration that Mr. Komsic speaks about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I did not read Mr. Komsic's book, so I was unaware of the fact that he was talking about that, but that is the declaration that I commented on a little while ago, and that was the situation that I was describing a little while ago when our side thought that a historical agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, compliments of the Praljak Defence team, and I must thank them for that, I am told there is a document that they have in the e-court system. It is 3D 00298, I just learned of this just this second ago, so this is all impromptu. I'm not trying to pull a fast one on anyone. If we can pull that up on the e-court, and maybe it's -- it's not in the binder. If we could pull that up on the e-court, and I believe it's an English version -- both in English and in Croatian, but it's been translated. And perhaps, Mr. Usher, could you assist our good witness to make sure that he can see it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, you can see it. Okay. I'm trying to micromanage the courtroom around here. Now, if you could look at that document. I haven't seen it, I haven't read it, but if you could look at that because I'm just told that that was available. Can you tell us with any degree of certainty whether that's what was referring -- what Mr. Komsic was referring to in his book -- the portion of his book which is 1D 01321.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, last time I saw this document was before I left Geneva more than 15 years ago, but I am quite certain that this is the document. I participated in drafting this document. I think that actually I myself wrote it physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then perhaps the Praljak team may have a question or two, I don't know, but we'll move on because I think the next document is a rather telling one. And this is 3D 00451, 3D 00451.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Still about that document which you have shown to us, now -- and after the document it was signed by Alija Izetbegovic, we find I think that it is the last page before the resolution of the Security Council will be coming. So -- and here it is written that this declaration is the first -- is the first serious attempt to stop the war conflicts between the Army of BiH and HVO and to normalise the relations between the Muslims and the Croats in BiH. Now, I -- is this part of the document, what Mr. Komsic wrote, or is it a comment from any other document? That is my question, that from which part or which document, if any, this -- in a way this assessment of the document is coming. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. This is a comment by Mr. Komsic. This is his -- Mr. Komsic, who was involved in various activities, but this is his comment to the document as well as the one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- that he talks about the secret -- the secret declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, 3D 00451, because you spoke earlier in one of the questions that was posed by His Honour that unfortunately two days later there was another agreement, joint declaration, signed between Alija Izetbegovic and Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. Is this the document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I think that this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could focus on paragraph number 5, paragraph number 5, and it says here, I'm going to skip a little bit the first part, and then the second sentence, it says: "This is an addition to the commitment already made to find a permanent solution to the governance of the Sarajevo district within two years. After achieving mutually acceptable resolution to the territorial delimitation" -- I guess -- "of the three republics within the union and during the initial two-year period of the union's existence, there shall be a provision for a referendum to be held on a mutually agreed date within the Republics of the Union on the question of whether citizens of any particular republic agree to remain in the Union or to leave the Union. "In the case of a dissolution of the Union, all the rights of the Union of the Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including membership of the United Nations, shall be automatically vested in the republic with a predominantly Muslim majority." Now, I want to focus on that -- on this particular passage. Could you please explain to us what is meant by this, what -- how it was understood by President Tudjman and others because I believe we'll come across some documents that clearly demonstrate that this became known, this became a topic of discussion, and you were aware of it, so I lay the foundation on that one.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we learned about this document immediately. After all the co-chairmen co-signed this document, the co-chairmen of the international conference. Our first reaction was that this was an attempt to cheat in relation to the document that was signed a mere two days ago because the Croatian side, President Tudjman, and I think that the same goes for the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, were not aware of this. Secondly, President Izetbegovic signs and agrees to the possibility that the Serbian side could leave Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is true that this option was envisaged by all peace plans, provided that it happened by peaceful means. But before that, nothing of this kind had ever been signed. And if I may, I would like to note one thing. Recalling the offer that President Izetbegovic made to President Tudjman about western Herzegovina leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina and being annexed to Croatia, if we were to put this into context of this document, the logical conclusion was that the Muslim leadership was trying to set up a unitary Muslim state with the Muslim majority in terms of population and that through this agreement it actually wanted to transfer the rights of a successor state to itself, including the right to membership in the United Nations. So that was our reading of this document at that time, and I have no reason to change this interpretation, that Bosnia and Herzegovina should break up. The Serb part could go wherever it want to, join whoever it wished. Croats should be convinced that western Herzegovina could either go independent and join Croatia, and then the rest would become a state with the Muslim majority, and this state would then be granted continuity. It would be the successor state of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it was before, and it would be given a seat in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, again, that was part of the question that you had asked, so if the time -- I could be given some extra time for that. Anyway. Okay. P 05155.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a presidential transcript, 17 September 1993, and I understand that you've had a chance to go through this transcript in the Croatian version. Not all of it was translated, but you were able to go through it, and as I understand it, you are mentioned in this particular transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to save time, is it also my understanding that where you saw yourself mentioned having read that part, you are convinced that that is not you speaking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I cannot recall whether I attended this meeting, but I can state categorically that I never uttered the words that are quoted here under my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you -- I'm sorry. You have said, Mr. Karnavas, that not all was translated. Could you point out what is translated because I seem to have a text which is entirely in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what was translated by the OTP, and I have here pages 48 to -- 48 and 49. That's what they translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you kindly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay? We attached the Croatian, so you have both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I found it. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it just -- now since we have the Croatian and the Judges have the Croatian, I wasn't aware that you had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now that you have it, could you please tell us what page number that's on in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatian, that would be page 01865828.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that's the ERN number that's being read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly, could you tell us why you think that is not you in the transcript speaking because sometimes the question is how accurate truly these transcripts are as opposed to whether they're authentic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person speaking here talks about some boards of management that I was never a member of. That person speaks about meetings held every seven or ten days, meetings that I could not have attended physically because at that time I was in Geneva. And this person mentions the name of the person who sat next to him last time, that is Mr. Fizilic [phoen], and I really can't recall an occasion where that man sat next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Judge Trechsel asked what was translated. Good question. Let's turn to that text because it might be of assistance because we have -- apparently the Prosecution translated for one reason. I would like you to look at that part, and this is page 48 and 49, keeping in mind what we've already discussed concerning the joint declaration between Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Milosevic. And if we could look at this, this part, 48 to 49, because it says: "You saw the position in collusion with the services from abroad" -- opposition. I'm sorry. I'm just getting tired -- "in collusion with the services from abroad who are still not in favor of a sovereign Croatia set the task of shifting the Croatian policy. "What for, if not to overthrow Tudjman. That's a bit difficult. That failed. Then to break the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, and with regard to that, they partly managed part of our people, too, a wrong policy on Bosnia and Herzegovina, as written. "As you see, the policy was not wrong. On the contrary, from the start, it was the only right one in the interests of both the Croatian people in Bosnia as much as possible and the Croatian state. As you have seen, he himself signed, after visiting the whole world, actually what he said, what he discussed with us in private in addition to what we publicly signed. We had talked -- we had talks and agreements that the Bosnian Muslim and Croatian republic was to go for close cooperation there, until later confederal ties with Croatia, et cetera, but also that the thing might develop in such a way that it would be better for them to be independent. "So, he signed it with the Serbs and made it public, so it can survive for two years at most. Now, look at the map of what will be the Croatian state, not just with the Croatian Republic but clearly it belongs to us, or the Bihac region, too, will be an integral part of the republic. "Therefore, Croatia has probably never been bigger in its history, but they raised the need for a shift. So the problem is in the completely wrong assessment by those who raised that. "Why do I mention that? I mention that because those people from those same circles gave directions not only to their own people but elsewhere that the -- that HDZ should and Tudjman in the area of the economy, that we should take matters into our own hands. In the interests of Croatia, I will not allow that. It is up to you. You are holding such responsible positions that you have to be aware of all those roads leading astray and all those wanderings. It is up to you to implement Croatian policy, which would upon the conclusion of the war with such borders which would be most favourable for Croatia, which would ensure, that is, economic sense, which would not create economic basis for the dissolution of such policy. Please keep that in mind." Now, in light of what we previously discussed, can you tell us if you can, what is Tudjman talking about? Because it appears that the agreement that was signed between Izetbegovic and Milosevic and Karadzic has now become public.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this meeting, really. I believe that I did not attend it. However, having read the whole transcript in Croatian because the small portion that has been translated into English, even if we disregard the errors such as the one -- such as the fact that I am listed here, it is difficult to conclude what this is all about. But this is a meeting between President Tudjman and people who are in charge of economic policy, enforcing economic policy in Croatia. So this is a meeting about economic issues, not political issues, and at this meeting President Tudjman makes comments about the political situation, about the opposition, as is often the case by -- with politicians. He comments on those who criticise him, and in this context he makes comments about the agreement that he signed with us that Izetbegovic and the agreement that Izetbegovic in turn signed with the Serbian side. So one should, I think, look at those excerpts in this broader context because his comments at this time are not quite certain because it is not obvious at that time whether the confederation that had been agreed with the Bosniaks would, in fact, be implemented, whether this agreement would be implemented or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, have a last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We'll skip some documents. We'll get to them through somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But one last document we can go through, and I invite the Trial Chamber to read it thoroughly and carefully, all of it. And this is 1D 02911. Now, regrettably, the time does not permit me to go into this. We would need at least one day for this particular document. You're mentioned in here. In this document, it touches upon the issues that you talked about, including the agreement between Izetbegovic, Karadzic, Mladic, the US's interpretation of what should happen, that they would prefer having the Serbs leave, but the Muslims under no circumstances to be on their own, there should be no Muslim entity in Europe. Could you please comment since you were there, I believe, and give us a full explanation of your understanding of this presidential transcript, which we will revisit with other witnesses, as well, who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended this meeting, and my recollection of it is relatively good, and I remember quite well everything that preceded this meeting. And I think, if I may be allowed to give my opinion, I think this is an important document because it is indicative of the final -- of the end of one stage in the peace process and embarking on the next stage. We, I myself and some other people, made some presentations to President Tudjman, but before this meeting took place, we had been in intensive communication with various states. I, for instance, was communicating with Mr. Redman from the USA. Our impression is, first of all, that the international conference was no longer a viable institution, and despite the fact that Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg were still the co-chairmen, it was not possible to find a solution through the conference. It also became quite clear - Mr. Redman, as President Clinton's Special Envoy, stressed this several times in Geneva and also in the region - that the United States wanted to be involved in the effort to find a solution. You will recall that President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic had urged the United States to take part on several occasions. I think that this was welcomed by our side, at least by our side. I met with Mr. Redman, and then I organized the meeting between him and Minister Granic about the month before this meeting took place. And we heard from him what his views were of possible cooperation between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, how he saw it. After a lot of debate, after Mr. Granic visited the Vatican, we realized that the time had come to renew the idea of stronger links between Muslims and Croats, and this was widely debated. Likewise, as a result of different information, different inputs, President Tudjman suggested to the leadership of the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina to make some re-shuffles in the leadership. I think that in this transcript of this meeting, there is a lot of talk about who would represent Croats, and it is quite clearly stated that the representatives should be the people who will not be seen as obstacles on the road to establishing good relations and peace. After this agreement -- or rather, I apologise, after this meeting, there followed concrete negotiations that resulted in the signing of the Washington Agreement creating -- laying a foundation for the Dayton Peace Agreement. I think it is important that in that agreement and at this meeting the principles behind President Tudjman's policies are clearly seen. He is concerned about the Republic of Croatia, but he's also concerned about the position of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he wants peace. There is another thing that is evident. I think that I did not really mention that, and I did witness this. The international community - I will be very frank now - criticised Croatia at times about its involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina, yet this very same international community consistently and persistently asked Croatia and President Tudjman to be the party involved in the effort to find a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not saying that he and all of us involved in this did not make any mistakes. Hindsight is a great thing, but with hindsight I think we can show this principled position in Croatia that follows from one agreement to another, especially here, because this marks a watershed in the peace talks. After this meeting and after the agreement that was signed after this meeting, regardless of the quality of this agreement, the final purpose was achieving peace, and this peace was finally achieved in Dayton, and this is the importance that I give to this meeting, to this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zuzul. I appreciate you coming here. We thank you very much, and we hope that you will be as honest and forthright with your answers to the Prosecution or to anyone else's questions as you have been with me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We are going to break for 15 minutes. We'll resume in 15 minutes. I'll give the floor to Mr. Kovacic, and we'll stop at 6.25 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. But we need the witness, of course. It's always a pleasure to listen to you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, Your Honour, my idea was to deal with procedural aspects before the witness is in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you would like me to, of course I can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in keeping with the instructions I received previously, I move that General Praljak be allowed to ask the witness a couple of questions himself. This will not take longer than 10 or 15 minutes. Questions will be about the siege of Dubrovnik, which is something that the witness referred to on a number of occasions, and also about the presence of the Croatian army in eastern Herzegovina in 1991. Related to that, a well-known event, the so-called Libertas convoy, which travelled to Dubrovnik carrying humanitarian assistance. Praljak had direct knowledge of this. He was involved in these events. He knew what was going on, and therefore, he has every qualification to ask the witness questions about that. Therefore, I move that General Praljak be allowed to ask these questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm going to consult my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, after considering the matter, the Judges allow you to ask questions but only questions that relate to military matters, not to diplomatic matters or other issues. But since you met the witness at a time when you were conducting a military operation, a military defence operation, I'm going to ask you to address only military-related issues because we know that the witness is knowledgeable in military matters as well. We know that from the presidential transcripts. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'll first be asking those questions, and there is something else I have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon, Mr. -- Professor Zuzul. That is how I will be addressing you from now on. Do you know that by the 31st of October, 1991, Dubrovnik had been under siege for a total of 33 days from the south, from the north, from the sea, and from the west as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time, because of that territory you talked about, in order to prevent a JNA attack and keep the JNA from penetrating further into Croatian territory towards Ploca and so on, Croatia was keeping some of its armed forces - I'm not going into the specific brigades now - in a narrow strip and because of that they had to across into Herzegovina and then straight on from there? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there was this necessity and that this was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know that at the time Veljko Kadijevic was the minister of the armed forces of socialist Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll be quoting from a book now. We shall be tendering this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] -- do you know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Praljak for interrupting, but again, as we start this phase of the case, I think it's important to establish the appropriate procedure. Your Honour, this is not cross-examination. This is a friendly examination. I don't think leading questions are appropriate. All the questions so far have been leading, asking only for a yes or no answer. This is not cross-examination. This is just further examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond, if I may respond, that is incorrect. This is proper cross-examination. He's entitled to cross, and in any system you can ask either an open-ended question or a closed-ended question or a leading question. In this case, he's been asking leading questions, proper cross-examination, and I don't see why the Prosecution is even objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you why. I'll make it very clear why because the way -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Scott. The Trial Chamber has issued a number of guide-lines that cover all issues. You can't really surprise us by raising a problem we never considered. In these guide-lines, we decided, we stated, that during the cross-examination the Defence should deal with matters related to the examination-in-chief of the Defence. But in case the accused deals with matters related to his own case, then we would consider that as part of the examination-in-chief and deduct it from the accused's time. Mr. Praljak has not said anything. He's practically said nothing. Let's just wait and see. The witness answering questions put to him by Mr. Karnavas dealt with military matters. We had the map. We had Dubrovnik. We are dealing with the military questions here. Mr. Praljak is now talking about Dubrovnik. That's part of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It makes no bit of difference what the topic is. That does not determine whether it is a direct examination or cross-examination. This is not cross-examination. This is friendly examination of a friendly witness. It is absolutely true, this is not cross-examination. On a direct examination, you cannot ask leading questions, and I would ask all the Judges to participate in this decision. This is not just a decision just for the President. This is a decision for the entire Chamber to make. This is not cross-examination, and the reason it's relevant is because of the way the time for the Prosecution questioning -- the time for the Prosecution's time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this comment. Let me repeat what I've said. Thank you for this comment. That goes directed to my heart. Before establishing whether he asked a leading question, let's hear him out. Let's wait for the end of the question. You are standing up, but we have no idea what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, Your Honour. Every question so far has been leading. Every question Mr. Praljak has asked so far has been leading, every one. Look at the questions in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the questions are back -- first of all, they're background information that has already been covered; and secondly, and I invite all the Judges to read books on evidence, there is nothing that says that cross has to be hostile as in hostility. You can be -- you can be friendly. I try it occasionally, you know, but you can be friendly in cross. It depends on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is not a question of the style. It is the question of what it is. Yes, I agree. I have been practicing common-law adversary system for more than 20 years. Sometimes cross-examination can be conducted in a friendly manner, and of course, I have done that many times as perhaps Mr. Karnavas has. I'm not so sure, but the point of it is that no matter what the style is -- we're not talking about style. We're talking about what it is, and this is not cross-examination of a hostile witness; this is direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The matter of deciding whether the witness is friendly with the accused or not is secondary, but let me go back to what the Trial Chamber wrote in its guide-lines. If the issue has already been dealt with during the examination-in-chief, the person conducting the cross-examination, even if that's a member of the Defence, is allowed to put leading questions to the witness. Secondly, if the issues raised were not dealt with during the examination-in-chief, then the person asking the questions is not allowed to put leading questions to the witness. The following example is given. We can take the following example. If he deals with Dubrovnik and Dubrovnik was dealt with during the examination-in-chief, then he may ask leading questions. But if Mr. Praljak suddenly decides to deal with a topic that was not addressed by Mr. Karnavas, for example, the ammunition, the calibre of the ammunition, then if he decides to do so, he is not allowed to put leading questions to the witness. This is part and parcel of our guide-lines. We spent hours and hours drafting these guide-lines. We thought that this could be a contested matter; that is why we drew up these guide-lines. Let him ask his questions. If he does not comply with the guide-lines, then raise an objection, and the Trial Chamber unanimously will go along with you if you're right. But at the moment as things stand, I can't say anything about his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, it is not cross-examination. You can call it whatever you want. This is not cross-examination. You can call it, you know, a blue turnip. It is not cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you -- Mr. Scott, Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Chamber wants to make that the policy, then I invite the Chamber to re-examine its policy if this is what's really intended because this allows someone to take a friendly witness and ask leading questions to -- is it true this, is it true this, is it true this, and that is not -- this is not cross-examination. This is absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'm going to give the floor to my colleague, but first, Mr. Scott, if you did not agree with the guide-lines, you should have asked for a request for certification against the guide-lines because obviously, the witnesses called by the Defence are not Prosecution witnesses, obviously. That's first -- and we all agree on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, why would you expect him or want him to attack the witness as a Prosecutor would if the witness is a Defence witness or a hostile witness? You want him to work under the same conditions as you, but it's not the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You can't hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I was saying that I'm not very optimistic about a fruitful continuation of this dialogue in this setting, and I would suggest, as there seems to be a different conception of what cross-examination means, that you put in writing to the Chamber a -- maybe a request for interpretation or for clarification where you set out your views, and then the Chamber can deliberate and give an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I will do that. The Prosecution will do that. We had stated this position previously. In one of the Status Conferences, we raised this issue, so it's not a new issue. I won't take any more time except to say that what the President said a moment ago in lines -- around line 20 and 21 of page 67 are exactly the reasons why it's not cross-examination. It's the questioning of a friendly witness by someone on the same side, and that is not by definition cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm really embarrassed to join this time-wasting exercise. I wanted to gloss over this debate, but I simply find myself unable to. Both Your Honours and my learned friend mentioned several times that I think three weeks ago the Chamber adopted a set of rules and guide-lines that were perfectly clear as to how this kind of examination conducted by the Defence would be seen. We are parties to these proceedings, the six Defence teams, and the OTP, plus, of course, the accused. We are here on behalf of the accused, needless to say. We have very thoroughly studied the guide-lines. This is a peculiar situation; that much is true. We are operating here in a mixed system when no one can invoke their own practice from national jurisdictions and systems. My colleague and I spent an entire day poring over this in a bid to analyse situations that Your Honours envisaged in those guide-lines. I'm sure you remember that we raised several issues or questions about one particular matter, and we weren't sure what the Chamber had in mind. We submitted a request for review or perhaps even an appeal if we went any further. This appears to be becoming a matter of style. A decision comes along; the OTP just ignores it. I'm not going into any of that. What I believe is this: The Chamber has passed a set of guide-lines, which is what the President has just said. It is our duty to read them and to study them. If we don't agree, of course there are legal remedies. There are mechanisms in place for dealing with that kind of situation, but I don't think it is ethically right to have this discussed in open court, especially once the guidelines have taken effect and have become final because nobody appealed the guide-lines. If anyone did, then it was us, this particular Defence. We did not believe that an appeal would be necessary because we were certain that it was a simple error. It was for procedural reasons that we were talking about an appeal, but actually we were asking for an amendment. Therefore, I think it is entirely pointless now to raise issues such as fairness or accuracy of this approach that was decided on by the Trial Chamber. These are biding guide-lines, and they have to be complied with in this courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, proceeded. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware of the fact that at that time, the 31st of October, the 1st of November, a convoy, a naval convoy was headed towards Dubrovnik named Libertas?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I do know that it was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Mesic led the convoy, at that time he was the president of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so, but I cannot be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now read an excerpt from a book very briefly, and then we're done. Mr. Mesic says the following: "I talked about Admiral Stane Brovet, cool, cold Slovene. He was Mr. Kadijevic's deputy. The only thing that I was completely sure about, Slavija 1" -- that's a vessel -- "must not enter Zelenika. If I allow that, most of the Croatian intellectuals and artists on board the ship would be arrested, tortured, mistreated, and perhaps even convicted. As for myself, it would be an easy matter. They would send a helicopter and just take me back to Zagreb. Mr. President, Brovet, goes for the jugular. We have reliable information that there are volunteers and weapons on board this ship. If that is not true, why don't you want to go to Zelenika? Let the ship be inspected, and everything will be clear." Mr. Brovet replies. "Admiral Brovet, do you know what it is that you are doing? You suspect your Commander-in-Chief, your president, of being involved in terrorism. The cold Slovene did not budge. He was malicious and cheeky, but he didn't want -- he was still polite with a thin smile. "Brovet: Leave that for your merry sessions of the Presidency, president, people are being killed here. There are no politicians' tales and one-upmanships here." Mr. Zuzul, this text was made public. It was published in the newspapers, but do you know that the commander of the JNA, the president of the Presidency, was in fact almost captured by Kadijevic's deputy and treated as a nobody?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: After you've read this, I do recall that President Mesic did make such statements and that such reports were published. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did this in order to show that the president of the Presidency and the Commander-in-Chief of the JNA did not really have a function at all. This is the command responsibility of a man of this kind. At the same time, this JNA was on the rampage in Croatia and before that in Slovenia. So now I've dealt with this, and I would now like to ask you the following. I've repeated so many times that this is a court of law and that the truth must be established for the sake of the victims. It is my inalienable right to contest the absurd indictment. And, Mr. Scott, you cannot get me to just lie down by force. I will not stand for the denial of my right to use my knowledge gained through the four and a half years of this war to let all this go down the drain just because somebody, for God knows what political reasons - and now we're talking about Madam Carla del Ponte - who claims that Croats as a people are --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] -- vile sons of bitches --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- the Prosecution. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, no, this is my comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have been allowed to ask questions relating to military matters. You have, however, now embarked on pleadings against the indictment, and I think you should comply with the President's orders because the President rules these proceedings and not you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you are attacking the Prosecution. Why? Why are you doing that? Because you had the opportunity to intervene several times before. Why are you doing this during the cross-examination of this witness? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, because it all boils to the fact that I have three minutes, and this is my life, my facts, my knowledge, my search for the documents, my truth that I have the right, the factual right to present before this Court, lawyers or no lawyers. I wanted to stand up and ask why I am not given the right to ask questions that serve your purpose, the purpose of finding the truth of all that. I don't want to face the guillotine without being accorded the right to defence. I did not abuse your time. I'm not saying superfluous things, but you, Your Honours, have to see that the president of the Presidency -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have been given the time as the Chamber ruled, and you have been given the time to ask questions. But you have not been given the time to make comments on Carla del Ponte's remarks and to use words which are, of course, not for this Chamber to deal with. So that is why I am saying that you had the opportunity, and I agree that the Chamber has given to you this. But you have in a way took more time to deal with other matters which are not within the ruling of this Chamber. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel [as interpreted]. I thought that somebody else would be asking the question. Thank you, anyway. I apologise. I do apologise, Your Honour, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I thought that somebody else would be asking the question or perhaps the Prosecution would volunteer the apology for what Madam del Ponte, chief Prosecutor, said in her book, that I'm a member of a people that is composed of vile sons of bitches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an interpretation error here because Mr. Praljak said something that is not recorded in the transcript. He said that this completes his examination and that he wanted to make a comment. He said: I'm done with my examination, and I want to address the Chamber. Nobody stopped him. He just kept talking. I want to deal with another thing. That's why I rose. The document from which General Praljak read the excerpt is in e-court. The number is 3D 01067. That's -- in English, that's page 3D 261917. In Croatian, original, that's 3D 261916 -- 06. The -- this document is listed on the Defence 65 ter (g) list. It's in e-court. It's a book by the current president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Mesic, and it is entitled: "The Citizen President." We would like to tender this into evidence for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the exhibit? You did not hand a copy of that exhibit to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, that is right. We did not provide this in preparation for the cross-examination, but General Praljak deemed that this would be a good time to ask the witness about this because the witness has knowledge of that, because we were not preparing for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can give it an MFI number, and once we've received the document, we'll give it a definite number. Please, Mr. Registrar, can we have an MFI number for this book mentioned by General Praljak, a book authored by Mr. Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Of course, every technical solution is a good one. It is in e-court, and then tomorrow, just like with the IC document, we will be submitting a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You do as we did during the Prosecution case. You'll have your -- you'll make up an IC list. Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you can start. I hope there won't be any other procedural problems. You never know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. For the time being, we don't have any procedural matters, but we will resolve any that might crop up as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zuzul, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: First of all, could you please tell the Chamber, and I think that our learned colleagues from the Prosecution would find this interesting. I want to ask you: Did I take part in your proofing for this evidence -- for your evidence here?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did I contact you? Did I let you know that I would like to meet with you before you entered this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- or rather, you called me once on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did I tell you on that occasion that I told the Prlic Defence about this wish on my part, but at the time when I called you I had not received any answer from them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So at the end of the phone call -- from the end of the phone call until your arrival in the courtroom, we did not meet -- or rather, we just passed each other by in the corridors here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, I thought that I would be questioning you in two parts. In the first part, I would be referring to what you said in your examination-in-chief, and in the second part, I would like us to try to analyse the procedures or the acts, the attitudes, of the Muslim delegations in the talks about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I would like to do that on the basis of the transcripts from the sessions of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But for the beginning, let us deal with what you said in your examination-in-chief. Your last answer to the Prlic Defence was that the international community wanted President Tudjman to participate in the peace talks about Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that many representatives of the international community, ambassadors, and so on, gave interviews to the Croatian media where they explained this, providing the following justification, that it is much easier for them to try and solve anything that has to do with Croats with one person, President Tudjman, and then let President Tudjman coordinate things with the Croats in Croatia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina; and secondly, that President Tudjman, in this effort to coordinate the solution of the problem in accordance with the wishes of the international community, might be more efficient than the representatives of the international community themselves. Are you familiar with those explanations? Do you recall those interviews?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were several such interviews where such explanations were proffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Antonetti asked you about the constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He asked you questions about the constituent peoples, if any, in the Republic of Croatia. Now, I would like us to deal with Bosnia and Herzegovina in greater detail for a very simple reason, to try and explain to Their Honours whether this issue of the constituent status of the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina was an issue that cropped up in 1990 as a topic that was important for the solution of the crisis, or was this an important question for the settlement of the relations in Bosnia and Herzegovina even in socialist times? Can you confirm that? I can ask leading questions, that the issue of the constituent status of the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a very important topic while Bosnia and Herzegovina was a socialist republic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as early as in 1944, Zavnobih - that was the land antifascist council of the national liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for those who don't know - in Sanski Most defined that Serbs, Muslims, and Croats were unified in the national liberation movement and that Zavnobih is actually the expression of the constituent status of those three peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1974, the preamble and the general principles list Muslims, Croats, and Serbs as peoples that constitute Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that several times; in other words, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact that at that time the three peoples were defined as constituent peoples but Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a federation, it is logical that to somebody not familiar with the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina might ask himself how was the equal footing of those constituent peoples ensured? Because we are familiar with it, we are more or less of an age, and we know how the socialist system functioned, I would say that the constituent status was ensured through the League of Communists of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the personnel policy that ensured that at all major political and economic levels there are representatives of all three peoples, Muslims, Serbian, and Croatian proportionate to the percentage of those peoples in the overall population. Can we agree on that, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not going into political analyses of how it was done, I can agree with you more or less that that's how the three peoples were represented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the League of Communists was the factor of integration, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but in the whole of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can definitely agree with that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that once the League of Communists was gone from the political scene, there was this need to resolve some issues, in this case the equality of the constituent peoples, in some other way? So once the League of Communists was no longer there, it could no longer perform this integrative function, was it necessary to ensure the integration of a state as such in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that now we have gone very deeply into the political side of the matter. It is my personal opinion that when a new state emerges and it gains sovereignty, it is necessary to define the position of the people or peoples in -- within this new sovereign polity, so I would say that I agree with you in general terms, but I think that if we would go too far in interpreting this in political terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree with the conclusion that the representatives of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina thought that if Bosnia and Herzegovina had a complex internal structure that would ensure that there were three entities based on the ethnic principle, there could be proper integration in Bosnia -- there could be proper integration in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection. I apologise, counsel. In addition to my ongoing and standing objection to leading questions in this fashion, just so that I'm not told that I should have objected when I didn't, and I am, and I'll continue to object to it, in addition to that on this particular question, I don't think -- this witness cannot purport to speak for all representatives of all Bosnian Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina as if they are all one single group of people all having the same view. That can't possibly be the case. "Can we agree with the conclusion that the representatives of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." What representatives? What Croats in Bosnia -- the ones in Tuzla? The ones in Mostar? The ones in Bihac? Which representatives? Stjepan Kljujic, Mate Boban, Dario Kordic? This witness cannot possibly answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, page 78, line 24, when you spoke of representatives of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you know how complicated it is. Some had varied and very different political views. So before you tackle this issue, ask the witness whether he's aware of the political situation of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ask him whether he is aware of the electoral results, what the trends were before you address this issue because Mr. Scott is right in saying that your question seems to encompass everybody, whilst the situation is far more complex than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, two explanations, the first about the nature of my questions. I would like to advise Mr. Scott to look at the questions I asked in the cross-examination of one of his witnesses, Mr. Herbert Okun and also Mr. Manolic. The answers of my questions, then, my theories and the answers that I expect are all entirely identical. As for the other remark, I entirely take it on board. I simply tried to avoid wasting too much time on this subject. I believe it to be generally known that in this courtroom that in 1990 at the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 98 per cent of the Croats voted in favour of the HDZ. If my information is not correct, I stand corrected, but I didn't think there was any dilemma about us talking about 1990 and early 1991 and that we were talking about the policies of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had my question been about 1993, I would have been very precise about it. I would have told you whether it was about Kljujic, Komsic, or Boban or somebody else, which is precisely what I'm going to do the next time we deal with the transcripts from the BH Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you're right, but from the very beginning in the matter of a few seconds, you could have asked him: Do you know what the electoral results were in 1990? He could have said: Yes. And then you could have started asking your question, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, yesterday and today you were examined by Mr. Prlic's Defence. You talked a great deal about the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation reached by Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic. This is P 339. It's in my binder as well. This is something that I prepared for the Chamber and everyone else just for the ease of handling. Mr. Antonetti asked a question to the effect whether this document was published or not; therefore, I prepared a copy of Croatia's constitution. Rather wasting any time on that now, I'll be asking you a very brief question, and I expect you to know the answer to that question. Articles 132 and 133 of the constitution talk about who was in a position to conclude international agreements. It is the president, and then Article 133 defines that some international agreements must be verified, or ratified if you like, by Croatia's parliament. As a rule, any agreements ratified by the parliament are then published in the Official Gazette. Can we, therefore, agree that the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation did not have that nature; it did not require verification by the parliament or publication in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my position at the time and now. I still believe that the president had the power to sign such a document himself without necessarily having it ratified by the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours wanted to analyse part of this Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation. In particular, I'm talking about item 2, the armed components of the HVO as part of the unified armed forces of the BH. I think His Honour Judge Antonetti asked a question about that very subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like us to dwell a little longer on that. If you look at my set of documents, you will find 4D 409. Mr. Zuzul, that's my set of documents. You've been handed the set. 4D 409, this is the decree law. I will be speaking as you're reading. "Decree law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Article 2 reads: "The Republic's armed forces shall comprise the army of the republic." I'll be continuing my question, and then we'll sum up at the end. If we look at the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation dated the 14th of September -- rather, the 21st of July, 1992, Article 6 reads: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is a component of the unified armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council shall have its representatives in the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Zuzul, can we agree that this Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation would require an amendment to the decree law on the armed forces, saying that only the republic's army was the armed force of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we agree that it would be necessary to enter an amendment to this decree law and bring it back in line with the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can we now look at 4D 410. Let us look at how the authorities in Sarajevo went about this. There is a decree law there on changes and amendments to the decree with the force of law on the armed forces, and then Article 2 is here amended, and it now reads: "The armed forces of the republic shall comprise the army of the republic. The constituent part of the army shall comprise the Croatian Defence Council as well as other armed compositions placing themselves under the single command of the army." My question, Mr. Zuzul: Do you believe that there is a considerable difference between what was agreed in the Agreement of Friendship and Cooperation and the amendments adopted by the Sarajevo authorities? Instead of making the HVO a part of the unified armed forces in terms of equality, the Sarajevo authorities say that the HVO is a part of the BH army. The other difference would be instead of having a joint command set up of the armed forces, the Sarajevo authorities hereby amend the regulations by saying that they are all under the single command of the army. Can we agree that there is a significant difference, in fact, between the agreement on the one hand and the Sarajevo amendments on the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is a distinction, also in terms of the spirit of the agreement and the phrasing itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything indicating that Herceg-Bosna's authorities considered this amendment by the Sarajevo authorities and took it to be a betrayal of the principles espoused in the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember anything about that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Prlic Defence asked you about the Banovina of Croatia and about it being mentioned in the preamble to the Croatian constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not at the same level as the Defence. We have in front of us a decree. Please look at Article 1, 4D 410. The way I read Article 1 of this decree, it appears that Mr. Izetbegovic does recognise that the HVO is part of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you have the same reading as I do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've never set eyes on the document before. I do, however, remember well the atmosphere and the debate about this particular segment. It was easy for both presidents and everybody else to agree about the fact that the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council would mount a joint defence. The essential issue was how this integration would take place. This is what I believe. The way it's regulated by this decree law, this is what the Muslim representatives were pushing at the very beginning of the negotiations. The HVO would become a part of it, but it would actually become part, be subsumed, by the BH army and not be integrated as one of its components. I remember that this was a much-debated issue at the time, and a compromise was reached to the effect that there would be a single army but not by simply having the HVO subsumed under the BH army. I apologise. I'm not really a lawyer myself, but I do remember the negotiations. This was a very prominent feature, and I think the way it is formulated here is headed in an entirely different direction from what had been agreed and eventually signed in the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what about deciding whether they would be integrated in a parallel structure or in another way? That's the -- what would happen within this structure. But you went to Geneva to take part in the negotiations regarding the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Could a negotiator from another country have said that Izetbegovic had recognised the existence of the Croatian Defence Council because he has integrated the Croatian Defence Council in its army. Would a Frenchman, a Dutchman, or whoever reach that conclusion after reading that text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you're entirely right. Were someone to show me a decree law like this, my first reaction would be that from a Croatian point of view there is a positive here. Mr. Izetbegovic appears to be recognising the HVO and its units; however, there is something else, and this is about the way in which he imagines the integration should go forward. Mr. President, we have been talking a great deal about this, and this was one of the most salient problems during the negotiations. Bosnia and Herzegovina, whatever formed, it would eventually assume, as a state, whether a unitary state or a state, that would meet the demands and needs of all its peoples. I think this is about nuance. It's about the nuance of the wording, and this is where the nuance of the wording is headed. Therefore, I think the interpretation by Ms. Alaburic is also correct. It's about unitary control, establishing unitary control, and not any sort of control where there would be equality. So I have to point out that this would be my interpretation too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] I thank the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're back to the Banovina of Croatia, and your answers to the Prlic Defence. You explained that the fact that the Banovina of Croatia was mentioned in the preamble was just what it said. It was about independence, it was about statehood, and another of its expressions was about the Banovina of Croatia. I don't think there is any dilemma about that. What about the 1990 constitution? There were opposition members in the Croatian parliament when the constitution was passed, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone ever in Croatia, as far as this is concerned, the mentioning of the Banovina of Croatia as one of the sources of Croatia's state sovereignty, would anyone link this to the purported territorial claims of the Croatian government at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not something that was ever suggested to me by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very -- fine then. Can we please go back to one of the Prlic Defence documents. Probably there, there was no time to show it. This is 1D 2039 -- it's also in my binder if you're looking for it, sir. I'm not certain, that might be simpler for you, actually. 1D 2039. You have -- you have the amendments to the constitution, 2001, here. Mr. Zuzul, who was in power in Croatia in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A coalition comprising several political parties, not including the HDZ, the party that used to be in power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore say that the elections took place in 2000 and the election was won by the socialists and liberal democrats who had formed the coalition?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these amendments were then proposed by the then-government, the social democrats and the liberals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, nobody in Croatia, not even the social democrats or the liberals who were in power, had any ideas about amending anything to do with this portion that refers to the Banovina of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I don't want to interfere in your cross-examination, but I'm comparing the English and the B/C/S of this document. In the English version, the second part of the document seems to be missing with Articles 1, 2, 3, and 4. Apparently, this is missing from the English version of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the Prlic Defence's leave to comment on their text. This document was prepared just for the preamble, the source. It was no one's intention to use the entire text, and that's why only the preamble was translated and not any of its individual provisions, the provisions of the constitution, I mean. I believe this document would satisfy the needs of my cross-examination in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, another question about the Banovina of Croatia and about the constitution. Mr. Stipe Mesic, the President of the Republic of Croatia, is believed to be an advocate of Bosnia's remaining intact. Do you think that he has the right to initiate any amendments to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But do you know that Stipe Mesic would have initiated any amendments to the Croatian constitution in order to have the part about the Banovina of Croatia thrown out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard about anything like that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: These proceedings are being interpreted. Could the speakers please be asked clearly to make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Ms. Alaburic? The interpreters are complaining. You have to make pauses before you take the floor when answering, and this also applies to you, Mr. Zuzul. When you have heard the question, naturally you immediately want to answer, but you should wait until the interpreters have gone through the translation. Otherwise, they completely lose, and we lose in the end, and everyone. Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, and while we're on an interruption, I would just again object similarly to this question. I don't think the witness can speculate as to what Mr. Mesic could or might have done. If he had a conversation with Mr. Mesic and Mr. Mesic said something to him specifically that the witness can recall, but he cannot speculate about what Mr. Mesic could or would have done or might have done in some situation. And a standing objection to the leading questions. Friendly -- leading questions to a friendly witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to Your Honours and to the interpreters for speeding up. It is -- this is what happens when you speak the same language. I did not hear the interpreter's remark because it was not made on channel 6, which is the channel that I'm listening to. I think that as far as Mr. Scott's objection is concerned, it is unfounded because I was not asking Mr. Zuzul about the intentions, desires, and so on of President Mesic, but I merely asked him whether he was aware that President Mesic initiated those amendments to the constitution. So I asked him about a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One explanation about the agreement between Alija Izetbegovic and the Serbs on the 16th of September, 1992, that you were talking about, that was document 3D 451 that you talked about with the Prlic Defence. Could you please look at 4D 1040 in my set of documents. This is an excerpt from a book by Miroslav Tudjman that contains this declaration. And at the end it is noted that this declaration was not signed by Radovan Karadzic but by Momcilo Krajisnik, and that it was signed by Thorvald Stoltenberg and by David Owen as witnesses, and that the original document does not have the signatures of Momir Bulatovic and Slobodan Milosevic. To avoid any misunderstandings about the signatories of this declaration, can you tell us, if you know, is this correct what Miroslav Tudjman says in his book about this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that it was signed by Haris Silajdzic and Momcilo Krajisnik as the plenipotentiaries of the President Izetbegovic and Radovan Karadzic respectively, but that's as best I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, we are going to stop here because I have a number of recommendations to give the witness with respect to the following hearing. You'll proceed with your cross-examination the following -- at the following hearing. You understand the situation, Witness. It was impossible to complete your testimony this week. You were witness to all the procedural problems we had to deal with, and the Prosecution has not even started its cross-examination. Furthermore, the Judges have a number of questions to put to you. You made the solemn declaration. You are under oath. You are a witness, a witness in the service of justice, and as a result of this, you should have absolutely no contact whatsoever from now on with Mr. Karnavas and with the other counsel who may examine you later or re-examine you as part of the re-examination. And of course, you are not supposed to have any exact with the Prosecution, who will also put questions to you later on. And of course you're not supposed to have any contacts with the Judges. If you're faced with administrative problem, then you should get in touch with the Victims and Witnesses Unit. They are supposed to deal with the -- your travel arrangements and make sure that you come back here on the 18th of July. As I told you yesterday, we won't be able to complete your testimony on Friday. The Prosecution will have five hours, but considering possible procedural incidents, that will probably take longer. Therefore, your testimony will resume on Monday in the afternoon, and then we'll be able to complete your testimony. That's what I wanted to say. If you have a question, please put it to me now. Otherwise, I'll adjourn. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, without trying the Chamber's patience too much, could I just ask that also the witness be -- it be clarified that not only should the witness not have any contact with either the Defence or the Prosecution, or as you said yourself, the Judges, but in fact with nobody, with no one, no other person whatsoever, any members of the Croatian government, any members of a political party, no contact with anyone about his testimony. About his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, excuse me. I think this is being a little bit unreasonable. Now, he can have contact, but he can't talk about the case. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: About his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that everybody should just calm down a little bit and just relax, but I think within reason he shouldn't -- obviously not speak about the case and about what was discussed here or what has to do with his testimony. But other than that, I think, you know, we would have to be rather measured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes without saying, and the witness who has held high-level positions is perfectly aware of that sort of thing. Please avoid dealing with your -- or mentioning your testimony with anyone. Do not say that you were asked such and such question and you answered this or that. But it's so obvious to me that I thought I didn't need to mention it. Thank you very much. We'll see you on the 18th of July. Thank you.
